Burry said that he expanded his Adobe holding at approximately $246.

Burry exited his Oracle puts and closed the last of his Caterpillar puts amid ongoing downward volatility in both stocks.

The investor is moving to donate a significant portion of his appreciated Alphabet shares, which he has owned since the COVID period.

'The Big Short' investor Michael Burry said on Monday that he closed some put positions while adding to long holdings including Adobe, MercadoLibre, QXO and Lululemon, and moved to donate a portion of long-held Alphabet shares.

Adobe Purchase And Outlook

Burry said that he expanded his Adobe holding at approximately $246, without clarifying the number of shares purchased. ADBE stock gained 1% on Monday to close at $246 after dropping nearly 30% year-to-date.

"I continue to believe Adobe will successfully adapt, as will several other large software names, to the changing AI environment," Burry said. He noted that free substitutes for tools such as Adobe's Photoshop have existed for decades, yet Adobe has still grown revenue by 10% or more in each of the past four years.

In his view, Adobe's advantage lies in its standardized file formats, large installed base, enterprise contracts, and information security rather than superior AI models. Burry identifies the main risks as the cost of using external AI models and the pace of new subscription growth, but he argues the current valuation more than compensates for those concerns.

Puts Are Getting Expensive, Says Burry

Burry also exited his Oracle (ORCL) puts and closed the last of his Caterpillar (CAT) puts amid ongoing downward volatility in both stocks. He continues to hold a large put position in the VanEck Semiconductor ETF, along with puts on the Nasdaq 100, Nvidia, MetLife, and Palantir.

He noted that his overall short-put exposure "continues to grow in size, so trimming made sense." He is now looking at using outright short positions instead of or in addition to puts, because "puts, with the higher volatility of late, are getting expensive."

Burry's Additional Long Purchases

Beyond Adobe, Burry added to MercadoLibre (MELI) at about $1,480, elevating it to one of his largest positions alongside Australian retailer Temple & Webster. He also bought more QXO common stock near $12 and increased his Lululemon holding at roughly $106.

Lululemon's next earnings report is not expected until the second week of December, leaving the stock under pressure from a continued lack of new information, he said.

For three years, the AI trade has been looking up to one face too often. Now it has an interim CEO. On November 12, Jensen Huang resigned as NVIDIA's chief executive and board member, hours after nerves gripped investors awaiting the outcome of the board's crisis meeting. And on an interim basis, CFO Colette Kress is running the chipmaker while the board searches for a permanent successor.

The board opened an internal investigation on November 8 after reports that U.S. intelligence had probed the CEO's ties to a Singapore data center executive suspected of funneling NVIDIA chips into China. A second reported affair, this time with a senior employee, followed. By the morning of November 12, the shares were down about 5% in premarket trading. Analysts were also cutting fast. Bernstein downgraded the stock to Market Perform and halved its target to $200, Baird cut it to Neutral with a $200 target from $500, and Morgan Stanley dropped it from its Top Pick list. Senator Elizabeth Warren's office has also asked the administration to preserve all records on NVIDIA's AI chip exports to China.

At about 11x forward earnings, NVIDIA trades far below the S&P 500's roughly 19–20x, even after 106% revenue growth last quarter. A multiple that low reflects the market's doubts about the sustainability of earnings. AI hardware is cyclical, margins above 60% invite competition, and a chipmaker trading below 5x forward earnings shows that investors are quickly pricing in a peak.

That is why money is spreading across the ecosystem: custom accelerators, the networking that ties clusters together, the clouds renting out compute, and the equipment that fills data halls. On the day Huang resigned, the leading GPU challenger rose 5.9%, and the biggest custom-chip designer gained more than 5%. title: Larry Ellison Has Lost $145 Billion in Net Worth Over the Past Year as Oracle Stock Fell 59% From Its Peak. Here's Why Oracle's Heavy Concentration in OpenAI Has Wall Street Nervous.
detail:
Larry Ellison Has Lost $145 Billion in Net Worth Over the Past Year as Oracle Stock Fell 59% From Its Peak. Here's Why Oracle's Heavy Concentration in OpenAI Has Wall Street Nervous.
Keith Noonan, The Motley Fool
Mon, November 16, 2026 at 8:29 AM CST 5 min read
ORCL
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The last year has been brutal for Oracle (NYSE: ORCL) stock investors. The company's share price is down roughly 44% over the stretch and roughly 50% from its high, and you can count founder and CEO Larry Ellison among those impacted by the stock's big sell-offs.

As of the company's most recent public disclosures, Ellison held roughly 1.16 billion shares of Oracle stock -- giving him a roughly 40% stake in the business and making him its largest shareholder. As a result of the large valuation drawdown, Ellison has seen his net worth decline roughly $145 billion compared to where it stood at his company's valuation peak.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Broader valuation trends affecting companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) industry have played a role in the stock's collapse, but the market is also concerned about Oracle's heavy reliance on OpenAI as a customer. Here's why.

Image source: Getty Images.
Oracle's massive OpenAI backlog is a double-edged sword

At the end of its last quarter, Oracle reported a backlog of roughly $664 billion. A company's backlog represents products or services that have been contracted for but not yet delivered and recorded as revenue. Of Oracle's backlog, at least $300 billion is widely estimated to come from OpenAI -- the company best known for its ChatGPT artificial intelligence model.

In other words, around half of Oracle's backlog likely comes from just one customer. While both Oracle and OpenAI would like to see the entirety of Oracle's massive backlog fulfilled, there's no guarantee these contracts will be realized.

If OpenAI falls on hard times, there's a major risk that the majority of its backlog with Oracle could be voided. The specific terms of Oracle's contracts with OpenAI aren't public, and it's reasonable to expect that Oracle would receive cancellation fees if OpenAI backs out of large orders, but there's no getting blood from a stone. Oracle has effectively married its future to the success and scaling of OpenAI, and it could face catastrophic setbacks if its bets on the frontier AI model leader don't pan out.

Heavy customer concentration presents significant risks because sales and earnings performance can deteriorate rapidly if a major customer scales back or cuts its orders entirely. The risk of customer concentration for many players in the AI infrastructure space, and Oracle in particular, is even higher due to the highly cost-intensive nature of data center build-outs and operations.
